meta.title: IPE knowledge network, c. 1976-2026
meta.description: Key works and theme nodes in top-journal International Political Economy, seeded from this repo's papers.json (Zotero) and supplemented with canonical works. Edges are typed relations with a one-line justification. Direction: source (later or dependent work) -> target (earlier or anchoring work); belongs_to edges link works to themes.

edge_types.builds_on: source extends or relies on target's argument or evidence
edge_types.challenges: source contests target's claim, mechanism or evidence
edge_types.qualifies: source adds a scope condition or moderating factor to target
edge_types.extends_to_new_case: source applies target's logic to a new population, period or domain
edge_types.synthesizes: source integrates target with other work
edge_types.mechanism_tested_by: source tests a mechanism implied by target

edges.why: Factor mobility decides whether Rogowski's class cleavages or Ricardo-Viner industry cleavages organize trade politics.
Takes the factor-endowment logic to individual survey data; skill predicts US trade preferences as Heckscher-Ohlin implies.
Replicates the skill effect cross-nationally and shows it flips sign in skill-scarce countries, as factor theory predicts.
Education effect holds among the retired and tracks ideas, so it is not a labor-market skill effect.
Sociotropic perceptions and out-group anxiety outperform self-interest; education proxies for ethnocentrism.
Extends the non-material reading of the education gradient with explicit attitudinal measures.
Shows most people cannot locate their own trade interest, closing the information gap in the self-interest debate.
Revives a material account at the occupational-task level: routineness and offshorability predict protectionism net of sociotropic controls.
Replaces skill and industry with task-based exposure as the material basis of preferences.
Adds occupational immobility to task exposure to measure insecurity at the individual level.
Uses import-competition exposure in the China-shock tradition as the shock component.
Status threat and out-group anxiety as the engine of trade-related voting.
Argues the 2016 vote tracked group-status threat, not economic hardship from trade.
Elite 'trade is unfair' rhetoric activates fairness beliefs, a non-material route to declining trade support.
Out-group affect extended to specific partner countries: allies versus adversaries.
Security externalities of trade reappear in mass opinion, not just state tariff games.
A spatial Rogowski model for 19th-century US protectionism, where trade winners lost political power.
Skill-based factor logic applied to preferences over inward FDI in Latin America.
Public FDI opposition turns on reciprocity and security framing rather than skill-based income effects.
Micro-level test: social spending sustains support for openness among the exposed.
Traces the full compensation chain at the individual level: exposure, insecurity, welfare demand, trade support.
Superstar-based trade theories imply far more losers than classical factor models predict.
Re-analyzes the Colantone-Stanig data, interacting the China shock with top-income shares.
Exposed losers from an external shock (franc mortgages) become attentive, interest-driven voters, as with trade layoffs.
Hegemony explains the form of the postwar order but not its content, which came from the embedded-liberal social purpose.
Re-establishes the openness-government link worldwide and supplies an insurance mechanism.
The openness-government link is a democratic bargain; it vanishes under authoritarian rule.
Embedded liberalism persists where left-labor power is encompassing, against convergence claims.
In LDCs weak labor cannot defend welfare, so globalization erodes compensation rather than sustaining it.
Compensation as the condition under which openness strengthens rather than threatens democracy.
Financial openness changes elite incentives directly, offering a second channel from globalization to democratization.
Compensation (TAA) blunts electoral punishment for trade layoffs at the county level.
Compensation and protection are substitutes: TAA-receiving counties demand fewer trade remedies.
Whether the compensation contract can be enforced depends on constitutional structure and geographic concentration.
Backlash occurs when the embedded-liberal promise of compensation becomes non-credible.
Embedded liberalism rested on excluding migrants from rights; inclusion eroded the compact.
Systematic review finds no settled evidence on why intervention retreated; disagreement reflects design choices.
Trade dependence shapes not only state size but constitutional design (PR, parliamentarism).
Institutional responsiveness to voters versus organized interests applied to labor-migration openness.
Interdependence constrains governments: measured as lower pledge fulfillment.
Policy (austerity) interacts with vulnerability to produce populism, not only external shocks.
Diagnoses the order's crisis as the dismantling of embedded liberalism by captured elites.
Reads the China-shock voting evidence as proof that uncompensated losers abandon the order.
Political consequences of the labor-market China shock: polarization and the 2016 vote.
Shift-share China shock applied to Western European elections.
China shock applied to the Brexit referendum.
Adds trade winners (tradable services) to the electoral analysis of trade exposure.
Long-run deindustrialization rather than the 2000s China shock as the shock of interest.
Racialized response: white voters move right, Black voters left, so the effect is group-status politics.
Trade shocks raise authoritarian values, linking economic shock to cultural backlash.
Shows 'cultural' authoritarian values have economic origins.
Status threat as the cultural mechanism behind the 2016 vote.
Trade shocks are outcome-significant but explain little of populist support's variance.
Integrates China-shock evidence into a theory of left versus right populism.
European evidence as the right-populist branch of globalization backlash.
Four mechanisms from globalization shock to right-wing populism, weighing economics against culture.
Argues economic causes operate beneath cultural expression even where variance explained is small.
Reviews attitudes, behavior and policy layers of backlash across economic and cultural accounts.
Places the cultural-backlash thesis alongside economic accounts and finds interaction.
Backlash reaches institutions only when entrepreneurs politicize it through permissive opportunity structures.
Place-based account of long-run manufacturing decline and populist geography.
Populist geography has 1890s roots reactivated by later globalization shocks.
Trade-war tariffs as a new geographically targeted trade shock with electoral effects.
A foreign state weaponizes trade exposure to pressure an adversary's electorate.
Confirms retaliation exposure cost Republicans House seats in 2018 and protection gained little.
Chwieroth and Walter extend the crisis-to-extremes finding with a wealth-effect mechanism (edge direction reflects later work building on earlier).
Insecurity pathway draws on China-shock political effects.
Three pathways framework organizes the globalization-democracy literature.
Inequality pathway specified through superstar trade theories.
Shock effects are mediated by fiscal policy choices.
Heterogeneous-firm theory as the microfoundation of firm-level lobbying.
Cleavages run within industries by firm productivity, not only between classes or industries.
Product differentiation plus firm heterogeneity splits industries over reciprocal liberalization.
Industry opposition breaks down in differentiated-goods sectors; Ricardo-Viner holds only for commodities.
Offshoring and intermediate-input sourcing, not export opportunities, define the pro-trade coalition.
GVC value-added linkages discipline tariffs, extending firm-level logic to policy outcomes.
Firm-level distributional consequences of PTAs confirm reallocation toward large, productive firms.
Firm heterogeneity in preferences across multiple dimensions of trade agreements.
Review of the firm turn in trade politics.
Supply-chain partners' interdependent preferences produce coordinated lobbying.
Relational supply-chain ties as a collective-action solution, here for lobbying rather than investor protection.
FDI creates the GVC-linked pro-trade coalitions in host countries.
Moves from FDI regulation to FDI's reshaping of host trade politics.
Supply-chain ties as an additional shield for foreign investors beyond nationality.
Diffusion through market access is conditional on markup gaps and lead-firm salience.
No race-to-the-bottom from export competition once spatial tests are specified properly.
Upward diffusion via lead firms coexists with the absence of downward competitive races.
Firm-level lobbying data applied to immigration adjudication.
Firms still lobby for high-skill visas even as low-skill immigration lobbying fades.
Credibility logic extended from regime type to international trade agreements.
Disaggregates PTA design to isolate the credibility channel.
Firms' stated priority on investment protection matches the FDI-attracting design features.
Nationality-based investor communities, not democracy, shield firms from breach.
BITs let autocracies substitute for democratic credibility and even prolong autocrats' rule.
FDI's regime-stabilizing effect operates through treaty-based credibility.
From individual FDI preferences to the political economy of FDI regulation.
Investment screening as the OECD response to party-state capitalism.
Screening as a concrete instance of geopoliticized EU investment policy.
Firm-level factor substitution (trade, mobility) reshapes the immigration coalition.
Monetary institutions as distributional choices among Frieden's sectoral coalitions.
Adds authoritarian subtypes to the domestic-politics theory of exchange-rate regimes.
Autocratic institutional variation applied to monetary rather than trade policy.
Sectoral preferences over currency levels plus state-controlled finance explain undervaluation.
Default is a domestic distributional choice, not only a reputational calculation.
The institutional features behind the democratic financial advantage also breed banking crises.
Capital mobility's constraint on governments varies with investor scrutiny, not uniformly.
Supplies a wealth-effect mechanism for why crises punish incumbents and feed extremes.
Eurozone adjustment conflicts read through creditor-debtor sectoral interests.
Market constraint and bailout politics integrated into one account of the euro crisis.
Privilege-taking via the dollar generates systemic booms and busts.

Collective G5 interests (bank exposure) rather than US control alone shape IMF lending.
Informal great-power access shows up as IMF favors for UNSC members.
Shared neoliberal beliefs, independent of US power, explain favorable IMF treatment.
Informal influence operates through staff anticipation rather than explicit intervention.
Routine reforms reward US allies but poor performance in non-allies triggers concessions.
Outside options matter only when overlapping IOs compete rather than pool.

Politicized lending generates asymmetric moral hazard and reserve hoarding.
Grievances with the IMF-centered order push states toward Chinese leadership.
Political allocation of official finance examined for China's overseas lending.
China's finance as an outside option with commercial rather than aid logic.
Autocratic IFIs, like regional organizations, defend threatened autocrats.
Autocracy-led lending allocated by regime-threat logic rather than donor intent alone.
Exit options and rival institutions discipline the incumbent IO's reform behavior.
From democracies' lower bilateral barriers to their greater propensity to sign trade agreements.
Democracy changes the form of protection (opaque NTBs) rather than its level.
Democratization explains the developing-world liberalization wave.
Among autocracies, institutionalization predicts openness as strongly as democracy does.
Flexibility (antidumping) deepens WTO commitments, as the escape-clause model implies.
GATT effects exist but only within the principal-supplier club of major powers.
Coding de facto participation reveals large GATT/WTO trade effects.
Specifies for whom the WTO raises trade: politically dissimilar dyads facing hold-up.
Security externalities become hold-up problems that institutions can solve.
Domestic political pressures explain WTO litigation as they explained issue linkage.
Beyond dispute resolution, states litigate strategically for precedent.
Participation rules in disputes are manipulated for settlement advantage.
Veto players condition the democratic propensity to sign PTAs.
PTAs as reform-locking devices for insecure leaders after democratization.
Credibility logic from trade agreements to IO membership during democratization.
Reviews PTA design, formation and effects.
Firm-level distributional effects integrated into the PTA literature.
Trade agreements' credibility effects extended to investment flows.
Veiled protection via state media as an extreme case of optimal obfuscation.
From veiled protectionism to veiled political retribution at the border.
GVC linkages, not only institutional flexibility, drive tariff commitments.
Takes the rehabilitation of industrial policy to the question of WTO discipline.
Rules designed for tariffs and escape clauses cannot govern subsidies and export controls.
Institutional (parliamentary vs presidential) variation in PTA liberalization at the product level.
Network topology replaces bilateral asymmetric dependence as the source of coercive power.
Reintegrates economics and security under unipolar network control.
Jurisdiction over hubs is the coercive face of the new interdependence approach.
Extends the framework across domains and catalogs its limits.
Book-length account of US weaponization of financial, data and chip networks.

Regulatory availability (safety standards) as the channel of informal retribution.
Trade punishment for diplomatic affronts measured in export flows.
Trade punishment exists but rarely buys sustained foreign-policy deference.
Finds little conversion of China trade dependence into policy alignment.
Asymmetric dependence produces foreign-policy convergence toward China.
Political tensions leave trade and FDI largely undisturbed, contrary to security-externality logic.
Third-party busting, driven by firms, as a reason imposed sanctions fail.
Threats matter more than imposition, here through protest signaling rather than concessions.
Financial weaponization provokes de-dollarization hedging by targets.
Empirical test of the overuse-and-backlash limit.

Informal coercion works through regulatory control over firms' market access.
Vulnerability to supply interruption drives China's energy mercantilism.

Economics-security integration driven by threat perception, now in China and the OECD.
Mutual endangerment between party and capital underlies party-state capitalism.

Structural power exercised as privilege-taking through the dollar.

Structural power as network centrality, measured.

Economic rehabilitation of industrial policy alongside the intellectual revival of neomercantilism.

Supply-cutoff fears can be overstated when markets adjust.
Asset-based interests extended to climate-forcing versus climate-vulnerable assets.
Decarbonization-driven trade restrictions as a strain on WTO discipline (contemporaneous).

LIO defined through its liberal-Westphalian tension, with embedded liberalism as its economic core.

Theoretical development and empirical demonstration of the new interdependence approach.
Transgovernmental networks as evidence of domestic institutions operating beyond the state.

Reductionism also lost the macroeconomy: growth regimes and crises.
Replaces state-strength explanations with coalitional analysis of international pressures.
International sources of domestic policy as diffusion among interdependent governments.

Globalization as an international source of domestic democratic strain.

Dynamic, system-level distributional politics against static collective-action framing.

Bilateral trade pacifies but multilateral openness raises conflict risk.
